title: A coupled-solver figure asks: did the two halves agree at their shared boundary, and did the iteration settle?
summary: Conjugate heat transfer and fluid-structure interaction solve two sets of equations that meet at an interface. The figures to read are the interface quantities (temperature, flux, displacement) and the convergence flag, because a plausible-looking field can be the product of an iteration that never finished.

Top right: pressure field falling from about 0.26 at the left to 0 at the right. Bottom left: interface displacement in a V shape, reaching about minus 0.009 mm at the middle node. Bottom right: tip deflection history falling from about 0.76 mm at 2 ms to about 0.01 mm at 10 ms.

read_the_figure.question: Do the two coupled solvers agree at the interface, and has the coupling iteration converged?
read_the_figure.axes: Each figure is a panel set. Field panels use x and y in metres with a colour bar. Line panels show a profile (temperature, displacement, stress) against position or cell index, or a history against time in seconds. The suptitle carries the converged flag.
look_at: Read the suptitle first. converged=False means the coupling loop stopped at its iteration limit instead of reaching its tolerance. Every other panel is then the last iterate, not a solution.

CHT figure: the fluid line (blue) and the solid line (red) meet at the dashed interface. Both must give the same temperature there (the legend says 399.41 K) and carry the same heat flux, so the slope on each side must be in inverse ratio to its conductivity.
The small grey text in the CHT corner names the coupling method (robin_robin) and the iteration count (n_iter=12). That is the evidence that the iteration ran and for how long.
FSI figures: compare the deformed mesh with the reference bottom (dashed). The flexible segment is the shaded band. Displacements of micrometres are invisible on a mesh drawn to scale.
The tip-deflection history is a convergence monitor. A settled coupled run ends flat. If it still moves, or turns, at the last time shown, the iteration has not finished.
Cantilever: the deformed mesh bends down towards the right, and von Mises stress is largest at the root at top and bottom surfaces and nearly zero along the middle line and at the free end.
read_the_figure.proves: A converged coupled run, with matching interface values on both sides, shows the two solvers have exchanged information until they agree. It does not prove the physics are right: that needs a comparison with an analytic or measured case. A run flagged converged=False proves nothing beyond what the solver was doing when it stopped.
if_wrong: Interface temperature or flux differs between the two sides: the coupling condition is not satisfied, so the iteration is incomplete or the transfer is inconsistent.
History still falling or rising at the last time: not converged, or physically still evolving.
Interface displacement and the tip history disagree in magnitude: they are measured at different times or in different units.
Stress contributions of very different sizes or implausibly small absolute values: check material properties and units before interpreting a decomposition.
must_check: The converged flag, tolerance and iteration count are stated, and the flag is true before any result is quoted.
Interface continuity is shown quantitatively: temperature on both sides, and heat flux on both sides.
Units are labelled and magnitudes are sensible against a hand estimate.
A reference solution (analytic or benchmark) is shown for at least one case.
The deformed mesh is stated to be scaled or unscaled.
as_drawn: Values are read off the plots by eye (about 5 to 10 percent).

CHT: fluid temperature rises from about 302 K at x = 0.002 m to about 399.4 K at the interface at x = 0.098 m. The solid line is nearly flat, from about 399.45 K to 400 K over x = 0 to 0.05 m. The solid is drawn in its own coordinates and does not reach the interface x-position.

CHT gradients: about 1015 K/m in the fluid and about 12 K/m in the solid, a ratio of about 86. If heat flux is continuous, the solid conductivity should be about 86 times the fluid's. The figure does not print the conductivities, so this cannot be checked here.

FSI flap, converged=False: the pressure falls from about 0.26 at the inlet to 0 at the outlet (kinematic units). The tip history decays from about 0.76 mm at 2 ms to about 0.009 mm at 10 ms. The final interface profile has a V shape with a peak of about 0.009 mm at the middle node, in agreement with the last point of the history.
Cantilever, converged=True: peak von Mises stress about 1.15 MPa at the root surfaces, falling towards zero at the free end.

Turbine blade, converged=False: the prescribed blade temperature falls linearly from about 1200 K to 500 K across x = 0.33 to 0.67 m. The tip history falls from about 0.72 mm to about 0.025 mm at 8 ms and then rises to about 0.08 mm at 10 ms, matching the peak interface displacement of about 0.08 mm. The stress decomposition has thermal-only and combined curves on top of each other at about 0.0007 to 0.0015 MPa and an aero-only curve near zero. A thermal gradient of about 700 K producing stress of order 1 kPa would be very small for a metal blade; units or material constants should be confirmed.

terms.meaning: Heat conduction in a solid and convection in a fluid solved together, coupled by continuity of temperature and heat flux at their interface.
A flow pushes on a flexible structure, and the structure's motion changes the flow domain. The two solutions depend on each other.
Each physics keeps its own solver. They exchange interface data and repeat until the exchange stops changing.
Each side is given a mixed (Robin) condition combining temperature and flux at the interface, which improves convergence of the exchange compared with passing only temperature one way.
Temperature is continuous across the interface and the normal heat flux leaving one side equals that entering the other.
A true/false report of whether the coupling residual dropped below its tolerance before the iteration limit.
A single positive number that summarises a stress state and is compared with the yield strength of a ductile material.
A beam fixed at one end and free at the other. Bending moment, and therefore stress, is largest at the fixed root.

remember: Coupled problems have two residuals: each solver's own, and the interface mismatch. Both must be small.
Temperature and heat flux must both be continuous at a CHT interface. Continuity of temperature alone is not enough.
In a thin conductor with high conductivity the temperature is almost uniform: the solid line is flat.
For an end-loaded cantilever the stress is linear through the depth (zero at the neutral axis) and falls linearly along the length.
A flag, tolerance and iteration count belong on any coupled-solver figure.

understand.title: Why the interface is the figure
understand.text: Inside each domain the solver is an ordinary single-physics code. What is new is the interface, so that is where errors enter. A CHT plot is worth reading only if both lines meet at the same value and with compatible slopes.

understand.title: What the histories show
understand.text: FSI is a fixed-point iteration or a time march. The tip-deflection history shows whether it is settling. A curve that decays and flattens suggests convergence. A curve that is still moving, or turns upward at the end, as in the turbine case, does not.

understand.title: Why the cantilever is the reference
understand.text: The structural cantilever has no flow, and standard beam theory gives its stress and deflection in closed form. It is the one panel set in the group that can be checked by hand, which is the point of showing it next to coupled cases.

steps.title: Interface conditions for conjugate heat transfer
steps.note: Temperature and normal heat flux are continuous. These are the two conditions the iteration is trying to satisfy.

steps.title: What matching flux means for the slopes
steps.note: The side with the higher conductivity has the smaller gradient. In the figure the fluid gradient is about 86 times the solid gradient, so a flux-consistent solution needs k_s about 86 k_f.

steps.title: A two-layer steady conduction check
steps.note: For layers in series the same flux passes through each, so the temperature drop across a layer is proportional to L/k. A high-conductivity layer has a small drop.

steps.title: Robin condition on one side
steps.note: Each solver receives a mixed condition built from the other side's temperature and flux. The parameter alpha is a numerical relaxation weight, not physics, and its value affects how many iterations are needed.

steps.title: Fixed-point iteration for partitioned coupling
steps.note: d is the interface displacement, F the flow solver (displacement in, load out), S the structure solver (load in, displacement out), omega a relaxation factor. Convergence means the bracket goes to zero.

steps.title: Convergence test on the exchange
steps.note: The converged flag in the title is the outcome of a test of this kind. When the iteration limit is reached before the test passes, the flag is False.

steps.title: Bending stress in a cantilever
steps.note: For an end load P, stress is proportional to the distance y from the neutral axis and to the moment, which falls linearly from the root to zero at the free end. This is the pattern seen in the cantilever.

steps.title: Thermal stress when expansion is constrained
steps.note: The standard order-of-magnitude estimate for a plate that cannot expand. A hand estimate like this is the cheapest check on a stress decomposition.

worked.title: Stress half way along the cantilever
worked.problem: In the cantilever panel the peak von Mises stress at the root is about 1.15 MPa. For an end-loaded beam, what peak surface stress do you expect at x = 0.5 m on a 1 m beam, and does the figure agree?

solution.text: Stress is proportional to the bending moment, which is P(L - x).

worked.answer: About 0.58 MPa. In the figure the surface colour half way along is a dark orange to magenta, roughly 0.5 to 0.65 MPa on the colour bar, so it agrees to the precision of the colour scale. The first cell is slightly below the root value because stresses are cell averages.

analyze.q: The turbine blade tip history falls and then rises at the last point, while the title says converged=False. List two explanations, one numerical and one physical, and one extra run that would separate them.
analyze.hint: Iteration limit versus real oscillation; halve the time step or raise the iteration cap.

analyze.q: In the CHT figure the solid line is almost flat while the fluid line is steep. What does that say about the conductivity ratio, and what would the figure look like if the conductivities were equal?
analyze.hint: Flux continuity fixes the ratio of gradients.

analyze.q: The stress decomposition for the blade shows thermal-only and combined curves lying on top of each other. What does that say about the relative size of the two loads, and what unit check would you run before believing the absolute values?
analyze.hint: Add the contributions, and compare with E alpha dT.

evaluate.q: Would you quote the deformation of the flap case from this figure? State what you would need to see first.
evaluate.hint: Converged flag true, tolerance, a refinement or a reference.

evaluate.q: A reviewer says the FSI mesh panel looks undeformed so the case is trivial. Is that a fair reading?
evaluate.hint: Think of the scale of the displacement against the channel height.

create: Redesign the CHT figure so that interface continuity is checked at a glance: show the flux on both sides and print the two conductivities.
Add a convergence panel to every coupled-solver figure: interface residual against coupling iteration on a log axis, with the tolerance drawn as a line.

checks.q: Why is it not enough to impose only continuity of temperature at a CHT interface?
checks.answer: Without continuity of heat flux, energy could be created or lost at the interface. Both conditions are needed: equal temperature and equal normal heat flux.

checks.q: A 0.1 m thick solid has k = 40 W/mK and a fluid film has an effective k of 0.5 W/mK over 0.01 m. Which layer has the larger temperature drop per unit flux?
checks.answer: Solid: 0.1/40 = 0.0025. Film: 0.01/0.5 = 0.02. The film has eight times the resistance, so it carries most of the temperature drop.

checks.q: A coupled run reports converged=False, but every field looks smooth and plausible. What can and cannot be said?
checks.answer: Smooth fields can come from any intermediate iterate. Nothing can be said about accuracy until the interface mismatch is shown to fall below tolerance. The fields are the state when the loop stopped.

checks.q: The cantilever has converged=True. Is it therefore validated?
checks.hint: What is the difference between verification and validation?
checks.answer: No. It shows only that the iteration finished. To judge correctness, compare with the closed-form beam solution (tip deflection and root stress) and show the agreement.

checks.q: How would you test a CHT coupling against an exact solution?
checks.hint: Two layers in series in steady state.
checks.answer: Use a steady two-layer slab with fixed outer temperatures. The exact flux is q = (T1 - T2)/(L1/k1 + L2/k2) and the interface temperature follows from it. Run the coupled solver and compare interface temperature and flux, and the number of iterations.
